sections.html: This species of carp attains a maximum length of about 60 cm, although specimens larger than 30 cm are hardly ever found in the wild. Common name: Assamese kingfish.
The species originates from the north of India, Nepal and Bhutan. The specimens currently traded are said to originate from the Sankosh and Torsa rivers in North Bengal.

This unique carp lives exclusively in clear mountain streams in the Himalaya, which flow to the Ganges and the Brahmaputra. According to the exporter, one can collect the species only a few weeks per year (August–September) and even at that time they are anything but common.
Fish of that size should be kept in large aquaria.
Hardness and pH are of lesser interest, but the species originates from subtropical regions and thus should not be kept too warm (14–24°C).

Almost nothing is known on the aquarium biology of this species. It is said that it can be best compared with that of Labeo-kind fish. This means that one should keep the fish in larger groups, for otherwise they may develop aggressive behaviour.

The IUCN Red List lists the species as vulnerable. The population has declined by 30% in the last decade and is presumed to shrink by another 30–50% in the coming decade. The reasons are overfishing, deforestation and pollution of the habitats. Collecting young specimens for the aquarium trade has no effect on the population, but due to the declining populations it is not very likely that the fish will appear on the ornamental fish market again.

Lexicon: Cyprinion refers to the relationship to the common carp (Cyprinus); semiplotum means "half swimming".
